content: The Latin phrase Primum non nocere translates to First, do no harm. It is sometimes alternatively recorded as primum nil nocere. This principle is one of the foundational teachings imparted to medical students during their education. It serves as a reminder to physicians to carefully consider the potential harm that any medical intervention might cause. The phrase is most often invoked in discussions about interventions that carry a clear risk of harm but offer a less certain chance of benefit. Since at least 1860, this phrase has been revered as an expression of hope, intention, humility, and acknowledgment that even well-meaning actions can lead to unintended consequences. The exact origin of the phrase is not widely known. Contrary to popular belief, it does not appear in the Hippocratic Oath. However, it is often described as a Latin paraphrase by Galen of a Hippocratic aphorism, despite the fact that Galen wrote in Greek rather than Latin. No specific mention of the phrase has been identified in Galen's writings. The closest approximation in the Hippocratic Corpus is the statement, to help, or at least to do no harm, found in Epidemics, Book I, Section V. According to Gonzalo Herranz, a Professor of Medical Ethics at the University of Navarre, the phrase Primum non nocere was introduced into American and British medical culture by Worthington Hooker in his 1847 book Physician and Patient. Hooker attributed the phrase to the Parisian pathologist and clinician Auguste François Chomel, who succeeded René Laennec in the chair of medical pathology and was a mentor to Pierre Louis. It appears that this axiom was part of Chomel's oral teachings. However, a closer examination reveals that Hooker did not use the specific Latin phrase or its traditional form. A detailed investigation into the origins of the aphorism was conducted by clinical pharmacologist Cedric M. Smith, published in the April 2005 issue of the Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. This study explored the origins and timeline of the maxim's appearance. Contrary to the assumption of ancient origins, the specific expression and its associated Latin phrasing have been traced back to an attribution to Thomas Sydenham (1624–1689) in a book by T. Inman in 1860. The phrase was also used in the same year in the American Journal of Medical Science by H. A. Stimson, who later referenced it again in 1879 and 1906 in the same journal. By the turn of the 20th century, the phrase was in common use, as evidenced by mentions from prominent figures such as obstetrician J. Whitridge Williams in 1911 and detailed discussions in a popular book by Dr. Morris Fishbein, the long-time editor of the Journal of the American Medical Association, in 1930. The article also reviewed the various applications of the aphorism, its limitations as a moral directive, and its increasing use not only in medical contexts but also in other fields. In the context of cancer therapy, the principle of Primum non nocere is not always the guiding tenet. The primary goal of cancer treatment is to eradicate the cancer. If this cannot be achieved, the focus shifts to palliation—alleviating symptoms and preserving quality of life while striving to extend life. In such cases, the principle of Primum non nocere may theoretically give way to Primum succerrere, meaning First, hasten to help. When a cure for cancer is possible, treatments may be pursued despite the certainty of severe and potentially life-threatening toxicities. Every cancer treatment carries the potential for harm, and some treatments may result in toxicity without providing any benefit. The therapeutic index of many interventions is narrow, and most treatments are administered up to the point of toxicity. Conversely, when the clinical goal is palliation, minimizing the toxicity of potentially harmful treatments becomes a significant objective.
